newsitem.title: JORDAN: Foreign buying of Jordan stock seen to rise in '97.
newsitem.headline: Foreign buying of Jordan stock seen to rise in '97.

text.p: Foreigners are expected to step up purchases of Amman stock in the second half of 1997 encouraged by a better investor climate and almost no restrictions on stock ownership, analysts said on Friday.

Investment managers say foreign buying, which has picked up since the start of the year to an unprecedented $56 million so far, should gather momentum after bold steps by the government this week to attract capital inflows to rejuvenate the economy.

In a sign of accelerated liberalisation moves this week, the Central Bank lifted restrictions on foreign currency transfers and the government announced plans to scrap soon a 50 percent foreign ownership ceiling on most publicly-listed stock.

"The foreign investor community has already given its vote of confidence and responded favourably by pumping in excess of $56 million into Jordan securities in the first half of 1997," said Omar Masri, head of Atlas Investment Group. "The second half should more than surpass the levels of the first six months.

Official data released on Friday showed an unprecedented 39.5 million dinars ($56 million) worth of stocks were purchased by non-Jordanian investors, both global funds and Arabs, in first half of 1997.
Global Western funds accounted for 57 percent while the rest was bought by Arab investors. In the whole of 1996 global fund buying did not exceed 9.6 million dinars.

Analysts say the latest steps could be a precursor to an accelerated privatisation drive and a planned state sell-off of a vast stock portfolio which accounts for 40 percent of the market's 3.2 billion dinar ($4.5 billion) capitalisation.

"Right now give me one reason that will not allow foreign investors to come to Jordan. Everything is set to making Jordan a magnet for their investments," says Ziad Basha, securities head at Jordan's British Bank of the Middle East.

Jordan's market price/earnings ratio (P/E) of around 13 percent still compares favourably with competing regional markets, analysts say. Recent aggressive Arab Gulf investor purchases which competed with Western-based emerging funds are also evidence of the strongest interest witnessed since the Gulf crisis of 1990.

Last month Arab Gulf demand surpassed global funds by 20 percent in buying orders worth 8.4 million dinars compared to seven million dinars purchased by global funds. This is partly attributed to mainly Kuwaiti investors who went on a buying spree on Jordan-Kuwait Bank stock.
Also Housing Bank has also successfully covered most of its share offering to double its capital to 50 million dinars, mainly by Arab Gulf investors.
A particular target of investors are opportunities in blue-chips which foreigners could not buy because their 50 percent ownership levels had already been exceeded.

Analysts expect global fund share of the bourse's total market capitalisation to rise substantially by the end of the year as a result of the stepped up purchases. It stood at 1.5 percent of a total 33.6 percent held by non-Jordanians, predominately Arab investors.
